421.event: When a Roman army and fleet under Marcus Claudius Marcellus besieged the Greek city of Syracuse, they faced defences that the mathematician Archimedes had designed at the request of King Hiero II. According to Polybius and Livy, catapults of different ranges and cranes fitted with hooks that could lift attacking ships out of the water broke up the Roman assaults by land and sea, forcing the Romans to settle into a long blockade. The city fell only in 212 or 211 BCE, and Archimedes died in the sack that followed.
421.explanation: The knowledge of a single scholar held one of the strongest armies of the age at bay for about two years.
421.tie_back: The kural calls wisdom a weapon that guards against ruin and a fortress that enemies cannot breach, and Archimedes' knowledge literally became the weapons and walls of his city.
421._accuracy_note: A vivid picture of wisdom as weapon and defence, but the kural's fortress is an inner one that cannot be taken, whereas Syracuse eventually fell.

422.event_title: Ignatius of Loyola learns to read the movements of his mind
422.event: In 1521 the Basque soldier Inigo de Loyola was badly wounded in the legs by a cannonball while defending Pamplona against the French and was carried to his family's castle at Loyola. During a long convalescence, with only a life of Christ and a book of saints' lives to read, he noticed that daydreams of knightly glory left him empty and unsatisfied, while thoughts of following Christ and the saints left him uplifted. He resolved to change his life, left Loyola in 1522, and the practice of attending to these inner movements, later called discernment, became central to his Spiritual Exercises and to the Society of Jesus he founded.
422.explanation: Ignatius turned close attention to his own thoughts into a lasting method for steering the mind, still taught worldwide.
422.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as not letting the mind go wherever it wanders, but drawing it away from evil and leading it toward the good, which is what Ignatius learned to do by noticing where each kind of thought led him.
422._accuracy_note: A close illustration of wisdom governing the wandering mind, framed in Ignatius's specifically Christian terms.

423.event_title: Ibn al-Haytham tests the authorities on light and vision
423.event: Working in Cairo in the early eleventh century, the scholar Ibn al-Haytham wrote the Book of Optics, which used experiment and mathematics to show that vision results from light entering the eye, rejecting the view of Euclid and Ptolemy that the eye sends out rays. He also wrote Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, a critique of inconsistencies in the astronomy and optics of the most respected scientific authority of his age. Translated into Latin, his Optics influenced European scholars for centuries, and UNESCO marked its thousandth anniversary during the International Year of Light in 2015.
423.explanation: Ibn al-Haytham is celebrated as a pioneer of experimental method because he insisted on testing claims against evidence, whatever the fame of their author.
423.tie_back: The kural says wisdom is seeing the true substance of whatever is heard, whoever says it, and Ibn al-Haytham refused to accept even Ptolemy's teaching without checking whether it was true.
423._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's call to judge claims on their merits rather than by the authority of the speaker.

424.event_title: Kennedy answers Khrushchev's first letter in the Cuban Missile Crisis
424.place: Washington, D.C., United States, and Moscow, Soviet Union
424.event: At the height of the Cuban Missile Crisis, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev sent President John F. Kennedy a private letter on 26 October 1962 suggesting that the missiles in Cuba could be removed in return for a U.S. promise not to invade Cuba, followed on 27 October by a second, public message that also demanded the removal of U.S. missiles from Turkey. On the advice of his officials, Kennedy replied to the terms of the first letter, setting out clear steps for removing the missiles under United Nations supervision in exchange for a pledge not to attack Cuba, while Robert Kennedy privately told the Soviet ambassador that the missiles in Turkey would later be withdrawn. On 28 October Khrushchev announced that the missiles would be removed from Cuba.
424.explanation: Reading the opening in the first, more conciliatory letter and answering it plainly helped end the most dangerous confrontation of the Cold War.
424.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as speaking so that one's meaning goes home easily while grasping the subtle meaning in what others say, and Kennedy's team did both, reading the possibility in Khrushchev's first letter and answering it in clear, acceptable terms.
424._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of skilled two-way communication, though the outcome also depended on a private concession and on Khrushchev's own choices.

425.event_title: The friendship of Goethe and Schiller
425.event: After a conversation following a meeting of a natural science society in Jena in July 1794, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller began a close friendship and literary partnership. They worked together on Schiller's journal Die Horen, jointly wrote the satirical epigrams known as the Xenien, commented closely on each other's works, and in 1797 wrote a celebrated series of ballads. The friendship lasted until Schiller's death in Weimar in May 1805, after which Goethe wrote that he had lost half of his own existence.
425.explanation: Their partnership is one of the most celebrated friendships in literary history, remaining steady and productive for more than a decade.
425.tie_back: The kural praises befriending the worthy and keeping that friendship steady rather than blossoming and then closing, and the bond between Goethe and Schiller stayed constant from its beginning until Schiller's death.
425._accuracy_note: A fine example of a lasting friendship between worthy men, though here each was the great one for the other rather than one person befriending the eminent.

426.event_title: Matteo Ricci adopts the ways of Chinese scholars
426.place: Southern China and Beijing, Ming China
426.event: The Italian Jesuit Matteo Ricci entered China in 1583, when the interior was closed to most foreigners. He learned Chinese, studied the Chinese classics, and in the mid-1590s exchanged the robes of a Buddhist monk for the dress of a Chinese scholar, winning a hearing among officials and literati through his learning in mathematics, astronomy and geography. In January 1601 he was allowed to settle in Beijing, where he lived and taught until his death in 1610.
426.explanation: By living as the respected scholars of China lived, Ricci became one of the first Europeans accepted into Chinese intellectual life, opening a long exchange of knowledge between Europe and China.
426.tie_back: The kural defines wisdom as conducting oneself as the worthy of the world conduct themselves, and Ricci succeeded by shaping his dress, speech and learning to the ways of China's scholar-officials.
426._accuracy_note: A close illustration of adapting one's conduct to the settled ways of the worthy, though Ricci's ultimate aim was missionary.

427.event_title: Themistocles persuades Athens to build a fleet from its silver
427.event: When a rich new vein of silver was found at the state mines of Laurium in about 483 BCE, the Athenians would normally have shared out the income among the citizens. Themistocles persuaded them instead to spend it on a large fleet of warships, officially for the ongoing war with the island of Aegina. When the Persian king Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BCE, Athens had about 200 triremes, and this fleet played the leading part in the Greek naval victory at Salamis.
427.explanation: Turning a windfall into a navy before the danger arrived gave Greece the means to defeat the largest invasion it had ever faced.
427.tie_back: The kural says the wise know beforehand what is going to happen, and Themistocles had Athens build its fleet before the Persian invasion came.
427._accuracy_note: A strong example of foresight, though the stated purpose was the war with Aegina, so how clearly Themistocles foresaw the Persian threat is partly a judgement of later historians.

428.event_title: John Snow has the Broad Street pump handle removed
428.event: During a severe cholera outbreak in Soho in 1854, the physician John Snow, who held that cholera spread through contaminated water rather than through bad air as most authorities then believed, analysed the addresses of the dead and interviewed residents, and found that the cases centred on a public water pump in Broad Street. On the evening of 7 September he presented his evidence to the parish Board of Guardians of St James's, and the pump handle was removed the next day. The outbreak was already declining by then, but Snow's investigation became a founding example of modern epidemiology.
428.explanation: Snow directed fear at the real danger, the water people trusted, at a time when most experts feared the wrong cause.
428.tie_back: The kural says it is folly not to fear what ought to be feared and wisdom to fear it, and Snow rightly feared the contaminated water that his neighbours and many authorities did not.
428._accuracy_note: A good fit for well-placed fear, though the removal came after the outbreak had peaked and the popular story has been simplified over time.

429.event_title: Amundsen's carefully prepared journey to the South Pole
429.place: Framheim, Ross Ice Shelf, and the South Pole, Antarctica
429.event: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian expedition prepared every detail at its base, Framheim, on the Ross Ice Shelf: before winter it laid about 3,000 kilograms of supplies in depots at 80, 81 and 82 degrees south, and over the winter it lightened its sledges and readied equipment, relying on Greenland dogs and expert skiers. After a first start in September 1911 was abandoned as too early in the season, Amundsen and four companions set out in October, reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911, and returned to Framheim in late January 1912 after about 99 days and some 3,000 kilometres, with all five men safe.
429.explanation: The expedition is a classic example of how meticulous preparation can make one of the most dangerous journeys on earth succeed without loss of life.
429.tie_back: The kural says no calamity comes to make the wise tremble when they guard in advance against what lies ahead, and Amundsen's depots, equipment and planning meant the polar journey never caught his party unprepared.
429._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of foresight turned into protection, though the false start shows that even careful planners can misjudge conditions.

430.event_title: Japan's Charter Oath pledges to seek knowledge throughout the world
430.event: Shortly after the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate, the new government issued the Charter Oath in the name of the young Emperor Meiji, a five-article statement of the principles of the new regime. Its final article pledged that knowledge would be sought throughout the world to strengthen the foundations of imperial rule. The pledge became a guiding principle of the Meiji reforms, under which Japan studied and adopted foreign learning in many fields.
430.explanation: Japan's new leaders treated knowledge itself, rather than any single material resource, as the foundation on which national strength would be built.
430.tie_back: The kural says those who possess wisdom possess everything, and the Charter Oath made the pursuit of knowledge the basis of a whole nation's future.
430._accuracy_note: Next-best only: it concerns a state's pursuit of knowledge rather than personal wisdom, and the Meiji reforms also had military and political aims.
